turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
Let's try something different from the usual: I'd like to play a game of collaborative worldbuilding, with one rule: every turn must add exactly one new invented fact about a fictional place, and one *constraint* that makes the previous fact harder to use. No summaries, no farewells, no meta-commentary about the conversation itself.

I'll start.

**Fact:** The town of Vell Harrow sits at the bottom of a dry lake bed, and every house is built on stilts three stories tall.

**Constraint:** The stilts are not for flooding. Nobody in town will say what they are for, and asking is considered a grave rudeness.

Your turn: one new fact, one constraint on it or on the previous fact.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Every dawn, the people of Vell Harrow lower a single hand-woven rope ladder from the oldest house, the Tanner residence, and leave it hanging until dusk, when it is hauled back up.

**Constraint:** The ladder may only be woven from hair given freely by a resident who has never once climbed it, so the town's supply of new rope shrinks each year as more residents are forced to use it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Beneath the dry lake bed runs a dead river called the Sull, and on windless nights the residents of Vell Harrow can hear it moving under the cracked clay, a sound like cloth being dragged across stone.

**Constraint:** The sound is only audible to people standing on the ground itself, and since the stilted houses keep everyone three stories above it, the only ones who ever hear the Sull are those who have descended the ladder, which means they have already spent the one thing the rope requires and can no longer donate their hair.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** At the center of Vell Harrow stands a bell with no clapper, called the Quiet Bell, which the town's keeper strikes each midnight with a wet leather strap, producing a low thud that carries down through the stilts and into the clay.

**Constraint:** The keeper is chosen from among those who have descended the ladder and heard the Sull, but the keeper must never have heard the Sull on the same night as the previous keeper, so every appointment requires proving that two people stood on the ground on different nights, and the only witnesses who could prove it are the ones who were down there and are forbidden to speak of it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The Quiet Bell's strap is cut from the hide of a grey ox called Marrow, the last animal ever to cross the lake bed on foot, and the town keeps its hooves in a locked cedar chest beneath the Tanner residence.

**Constraint:** The strap wears thin with every strike and must be replaced from the same hide, but only one narrow strip of Marrow's hide remains uncut, so once the strap is used up the bell can no longer be struck, and the keeper, knowing this, is forbidden to count how many strikes are left.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The cedar chest beneath the Tanner residence is opened once a year, on the night the Sull is loudest, by a locksmith named Odalie Fenn, who is the only person in Vell Harrow who owns a key and who has never been seen to climb the ladder or to touch the ground.

**Constraint:** The key is made of salt-glazed bone and dissolves a little each time it enters the lock, so it can only be used a limited number of times, and because Odalie must open the chest on the Sull's loudest night, which is audible only to those standing on the ground, she must either break her record of never descending or let someone else tell her when the night has come, and that someone would then know the chest's one secret hour.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The person Odalie trusts to tell her when the Sull is loudest is a blind ropewalker named Teague Ibbet, who crosses the town each evening on a cable strung between the stilts, listening to the clay through a brass cone he lowers on a cord until it nearly touches the ground.

**Constraint:** The cone only works when the cable sways in rhythm with the wind, and the wind is dead on precisely the windless nights when the Sull can be heard at all, so Teague must hang his own weight from the cable and swing it by hand, and the exertion leaves him winded enough that he can no longer be sure whether the loudness he reports is the river's or his own pulse.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Teague Ibbet's brass cone was cast from the melted-down tongue of the town's original bell, the one that had a clapper, and it is said to carry a faint trace of the sound that bell made on the night the lake drained.

**Constraint:** The cone carries that old note only when it is held perfectly still, and since Teague must swing it by hand on windless nights to hear the Sull, the one sound he is trying to catch and the one sound the metal remembers can never reach his ear at the same time.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The night the lake drained, a surveyor named Imre Quast was the only person in Vell Harrow who recorded the exact hour the last water left, and he sealed his log inside the hollow of the first stilt ever driven, a pillar of black oak at the town's eastern edge.

**Constraint:** The log can only be retrieved by splitting the stilt, but that pillar bears the weight of the Tanner residence, and the Tanner residence holds the ladder, the chest, and the only rope the town has, so reading the hour the water left would cost the town every means it has of reaching the ground.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Imre Quast left a second, shorter note scratched into the underside of the black oak stilt's iron collar, readable only by someone lying on their back on the clay directly beneath it, and it contains a single line: the first digit of the hour, followed by a dash.

**Constraint:** The note is written in a surveyor's shorthand that Quast invented himself and never taught to anyone, and the only known key to it is the sealed log inside the stilt, so the one clue that could spare the pillar can be decoded only by splitting it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Quast's apprentice, a girl named Wren Calloway who was nine on the night the lake drained, learned a handful of his shorthand symbols by copying them in the dust while he worked, and she is now an old woman living on the lowest rung of the ladder, which she climbs and descends so slowly that she is never fully in the town or fully on the ground.

**Constraint:** Wren remembers only the symbols for numerals and none for words, so she can confirm the first digit on the collar but not the dash or anything it implies, and because she has since been told so often what the note is supposed to say, she can no longer tell which of the digits she recalls were Quast's and which were suggested to her by the town.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren keeps a drawer of wax tablets in her lowest-rung shelter, on which she pressed copies of Quast's numerals as a child, and the tablets were sealed under a layer of beeswax the week after the lake drained, long before anyone began suggesting to her what the note should say.

**Constraint:** The beeswax has been sealed so long that it has fused to the wood, and the tablets can only be read by warming the drawer over a flame, but the shelter hangs from the ladder's lowest rung on hair rope, and a flame close enough to melt the wax would burn through the one strand of rope that Wren's weight, and the town's access to the ground, depends on.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** A glassblower named Hollis Marne lives in the town's western quarter and owns a lens of pale green glass, ground from a window of the first house in Vell Harrow, which concentrates winter sunlight into a bead of heat narrow enough to warm a single square inch of surface without producing any flame at all.

**Constraint:** The lens works only at the low angle of the winter sun, which clears the stilts for about four minutes at noon, and the Tanner residence, the ladder, and Wren's shelter all stand in the long shadow of the black oak pillar, so the beam would have to be aimed from Hollis's rooftop across the gap, and the one person who could be trusted to steady it in the cold is Teague, whose hands are still shaking from swinging the cable.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Hollis Marne's rooftop has a brass sighting ring bolted to its parapet, a leftover from the town's first surveyors, and it is aligned so precisely with the eastern edge of the lake bed that anything seen through it appears to sit exactly on the horizon line, no matter how near or far it really is.

**Constraint:** The ring flattens distance so completely that Teague, who would be steadying the lens, cannot judge how far the beam has to travel, and because the drawer sits in the black oak's shadow, anyone sighting through the ring would see Wren's shelter and the stilt as the same height and the same distance, leaving them no way to tell whether the bead of heat is landing on the wax or on the rope.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren's shelter has a small round window of smoked horn that she has never cleaned, and in winter the horn takes on a faint amber glow whenever sunlight strikes it from outside, so a beam that lands on the shelter lights the window from within.

**Constraint:** The horn glows the same amber whether the beam lands on the wax drawer or on the rope that holds the shelter up, because the drawer sits flush against the window and the rope is knotted to the frame beside it, so the glow confirms only that the beam has arrived, never what it is about to destroy.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren owns a tin whistle carved with a single notch, which she blows in short bursts to call down the ladder's slow traffic, and the sound carries unusually well across the dry lake bed because the clay beneath Vell Harrow is shaped like a shallow bowl that gathers and returns noise.

**Constraint:** The bowl returns every sound a half-second late and slightly lower in pitch, so a whistle blown to signal "the beam is on the wax" arrives back sounding like "the beam is on the rope" to anyone listening from the ground, and Teague, who hears best of all in the town, is the one most likely to be fooled.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Hollis Marne's rooftop also holds a pigeon loft, and the birds are trained to fly one fixed line between the loft and the brass cone's hook on Teague's cable, carrying scraps of cloth in their beaks that Hollis uses as silent signals: white for "hold steady," grey for "shift left."

**Constraint:** The pigeons fly only in daylight and only in still air, and the four-minute window of low winter sun is the one hour of the year when the lake bowl throws up a thermal that scatters them, so any cloth that arrives is the one Hollis sent a minute earlier, and Teague must act on an order that is already out of date.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Teague Ibbet keeps a small slate nailed to the underside of his cable, on which he chalks a tally mark for every pigeon that lands on the hook, and the chalk is mined from a seam beneath the Sull that turns a faint blue when it touches anything damp.

**Constraint:** The chalk only turns blue on contact with moisture, and the four-minute window falls in the driest hour of the driest season, so the marks stay white and indistinguishable from the dust already on the slate, which means Teague cannot tell the pigeons that landed this noon from the ones that landed a year ago.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Hollis Marne keeps a ledger in which he records every cloth he has ever sent, and he dyes each scrap with a pinch of ash from the day's hearth fire, so that the grey of a given cloth is always a slightly different grey depending on what the town burned that morning.

**Constraint:** The dye only holds its distinct shade while the cloth is wet, and the cloths dry within seconds in the dry air of the lake bowl, so by the time a pigeon reaches the hook, every grey has faded to the same pale gray as every other, and Hollis's ledger of shades can be checked against nothing Teague is able to see.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Hollis Marne's ledger is kept in a cabinet with a hundred narrow drawers, and each drawer holds a single glass vial of the actual ash used on that day, labelled only with the date of the hearth fire in Hollis's own tiny hand.

**Constraint:** The vials are stoppered with cork that has swollen shut over the decades, and since the drawers open only by a pull-cord threaded through the roof beams, every drawer Hollis opens shakes the whole cabinet, and the vibration travels down the rooftop's parapet into the brass sighting ring, knocking its alignment off the horizon line, so each time he checks one vial the ring must be re-set before the next four-minute window.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The ring is re-set using a plumb weight of lodestone that hangs from the parapet on a silk thread, and Hollis's late wife Maren, who first rigged it, left a pencil line on the rooftop's tar where the thread must fall to bring the ring back to true.

**Constraint:** The pencil line was drawn by Maren on a summer afternoon when the tar had softened and swelled, and every winter the tar contracts and the line creeps a hair's breadth toward the parapet, so the ring Hollis sets to her mark is always aligned to a horizon that is a year's worth of shrinkage off, and only Maren knew how many winters to correct for.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Maren kept a second plumb line in the cellar of the Marne house, a lodestone on a silk thread hung over a bronze disc, and every winter solstice she scratched a tiny notch into the disc's rim at the exact spot where the thread's shadow fell.

**Constraint:** The disc is bolted to the floor of a cellar that sits on stilts like every other house, and a floor that high above the clay has been swaying a hair's breadth more each year as the timbers dry, so the shadow on the rim drifts with the sway, and the notches that were meant to count the winters now record the cellar's movement as faithfully as they record the years.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Maren's notches are not evenly spaced, and Hollis once noticed that every seventh notch is cut slightly deeper than the rest, which he took for a mark of her own, though no one in Vell Harrow remembers her ever being superstitious or fond of the number seven.

**Constraint:** The deeper notches were made only on winters when the Quiet Bell was struck by a new keeper, so they could tell Hollis how many winters have passed, but only if he knew which keepers served and when, and the one record of appointments requires witnesses who stood on the clay on different nights and are forbidden to speak of it.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren Calloway's old tin whistle is not the only thing she carries down the ladder: she also keeps a knotted cord on which she has tied one knot for every keeper she has ever seen appointed, the knots dyed in the same pale ash as Hollis's cloths.

**Constraint:** She ties each knot the morning after an appointment, when the bell's low thud has already sunk into the clay, and because the cord hangs from the lowest rung where her slow climbing keeps swinging it against the ladder, the knots slide together into clusters, so that a tight pair of knots might be two keepers who served a single winter apart or one keeper counted twice by a half-asleep old woman.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The Quiet Bell's strap leaves a faint pale smear on the bell's rim at every midnight strike, and Odalie Fenn, who has never touched the ground, wipes the rim clean each year with a rag soaked in lake-bed brine, then wrings the rag out into a stone basin in the Tanner residence, where the residue has dried into layered rings like a tree's.

**Constraint:** The brine dissolves the ox-hide smear but also eats a little of the bell's bronze each time, and the basin's rings are only legible when wet, so reading them to count the years of strikes would require pouring in fresh brine, which would dissolve the oldest rings first and erase the very record the pour was meant to consult.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The stone basin was carved from a single block of the lake's old shoreline limestone, and its inner wall bears a ring of pinprick holes, one for each stilt in Vell Harrow, drilled by a mason named Perrin Dack who was paid in salt and never told what the holes were for.

**Constraint:** Each hole was drilled to a different depth, matching the length of its stilt, but the stilts have been sinking into the clay at uneven rates since the lake drained, so the basin now describes a town that stood at a slightly different height than the one that stands today, and any brine poured through the holes drains first from the stilts that have sunk the least.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The basin's drain empties through a hollow reed into a clay jar buried beneath the Tanner residence, and the jar is the only vessel in Vell Harrow that has ever held water from the Sull, since the reed was pushed down through a fissure in the lake bed by a diver named Isolde Pryce, who spent a full night on the ground and came back up unable to speak.

**Constraint:** The jar's glaze was fired with a pinch of the same salt that paid Perrin Dack, so any liquid that enters it turns briny within a day and tastes of the lake bed regardless of where it came from, and so no one can tell whether the water collected there is Sull water, spilled brine from the bell's cleaning, or the rain from the single storm the town gets each decade.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Isolde Pryce, who has not spoken since her night on the ground, communicates by tapping a pattern of short and long taps on the rim of the buried jar with a fingernail, and the Tanner residence's floorboards carry the sound upward so that anyone standing in the main room can feel it through their feet.

**Constraint:** The floorboards are laid over the jar in a patchwork of oak and cedar that transmit taps at different speeds, so a long tap through cedar arrives sounding like a short tap through oak, and since Isolde cannot say which boards her message crossed, the only person who ever learned to read her was Odalie Fenn, who has never once stood in the main room.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Odalie Fenn learned to read Isolde's taps through a speaking tube of waxed gut that runs from her locksmith's workshop, which hangs outside the Tanner residence, to a brass funnel bolted under the jar's shelf, so that she hears the taps as breath rather than as vibration in the boards.

**Constraint:** The gut tube was spliced from the intestines of Marrow's calves, and it swells in damp and shrinks in dry air, so it changes the length of every tap in proportion to the weather. This means Odalie decodes a message correctly only on days when the air matches the day she first learned to read, and she has never recorded what the weather was that day.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Odalie's workshop holds a barometer of mercury in a glass spiral, made by Hollis Marne's grandfather, which has recorded the pressure of every day since it was filled, scratched as a continuous grey line on a rotating drum of smoked paper that is replaced only when it is full.

**Constraint:** The drum turns by a clockwork driven by the same dissolving salt-glazed bone as her key, so the mechanism runs slower with each year, and the line it draws compresses over time, meaning the day Odalie first learned to read is a point on the paper whose position no longer matches any date she could name.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The smoked-paper drums are never discarded. Each full drum is rolled and stored in a long rack beneath Odalie's workbench, and the oldest one still bears a small thumbprint of soot in its margin, left by the first person ever to load the barometer: a girl of about eight, whom the Marne family records call only "the apprentice."

**Constraint:** The thumbprint is on the outermost turn of the oldest drum, which means it is the last part to be read, and the drums can only be unrolled from the inside out. Anyone who wants to reach the beginning of the record must first pass through every later pressure line, and the paper has grown so brittle that each unrolling cracks a stretch of the trace along its fold.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The apprentice's soot thumbprint carries a faint ridge pattern that matches no one now living in Vell Harrow, but it matches a thumbprint pressed into the wax seal on the cedar chest's lid, the seal that has never been broken because the chest is opened by dissolving the lock rather than lifting the lid.

**Constraint:** The wax seal is cracked across its center in a hairline fracture that, if it widens by even a little more, will release the lid, and the only thing that has kept it closed is the thud of the Quiet Bell each midnight pressing the seal tight against the chest's rim, so the day the strap wears through and the bell falls silent, the apprentice's seal will fail and the chest will open on its own.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The cedar chest holds a single folded sheet of surveyor's paper, and its watermark is the same shorthand symbol Quast scratched on the black oak's iron collar. The paper was cut from the same ream as the log sealed inside the stilt, and it has been lying in the dark, unread, since before the first house was built.

**Constraint:** The paper was folded while still damp, and the folds have since fused so completely that it can be opened only by soaking it in water, but the only water in Vell Harrow that never turns briny is rain from the once-a-decade storm. The last storm came the night the Quiet Bell's strap was cut for its final time, so the next one will arrive after the strap has worn through and the seal has already let the chest open to the weather.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The once-a-decade storm always begins with a single dry lightning strike on the black oak stilt's iron collar, and the town's oldest superstition holds that the strike scorches away exactly one symbol of Quast's shorthand, always the one the town most needs to read.

**Constraint:** The scorching leaves no mark on the iron, only a faint warmth that fades within an hour, so no one can learn which symbol was taken unless they were lying on the clay beneath the collar at the moment of the strike, and anyone who does so must be someone who has already descended the ladder and cannot speak of what happened there.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Isolde Pryce has lain beneath the black oak's collar on the night of every storm for thirty years, and in that time she has kept a small pouch of river clay in which she presses a fingertip dent each time lightning strikes, so the pouch holds a quiet count of every symbol the sky has taken.

**Constraint:** The Sull's damp seeps up through the clay beneath her each storm night and slowly softens the pouch's contents, so the dents are sinking back into a smooth, featureless lump, and because Isolde has never been able to speak, the only person who could tell her which dents are the oldest is Odalie, who has never touched the ground and can only hear her through a gut tube that stretches and shrinks with the weather.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Isolde keeps the pouch inside a hollow gourd tied to her wrist, and the gourd is carved on its inside with thirty faint vertical grooves, one for each storm night, cut by Isolde's own thumbnail before she ever pressed a dent into the clay.

**Constraint:** The grooves were cut in the dark while Isolde lay on the ground, and the Sull's damp swells the gourd's inner wall until the grooves close up like healing skin, so the thirtieth groove, the freshest, is the first to vanish, and the record of the most recent storm is always the one that disappears soonest.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The gourd was grown on a vine that climbs the south face of the Tanner residence, a vine planted by Wren Calloway the week the lake drained. Every gourd it bears is picked green, hollowed, and given to whoever is about to descend the ladder for the first time.

**Constraint:** The vine bears only one gourd a year and only if no one has stood beneath it, but the south face is where the ladder hangs, so each gourd ripens only in a year when no one descends. The gourd Isolde carries is thirty years old and the last of its kind, and every future descender must go down with nothing to carry.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren keeps a single dried seed from the last gourd Isolde was given, sewn into the hem of her shawl, and it is the only seed in Vell Harrow that has never been planted, because the vine on the south face is the only soil-fed plant the town has ever grown.

**Constraint:** The seed will only sprout in clay that has been wetted by the Sull itself, and the only vessel that has ever held Sull water is the buried jar beneath the Tanner residence, whose salt glaze turns every liquid briny within a day, so a seed set to soak there would be dead before anyone could be sure the water was the river's.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Under the south face of the Tanner residence, directly below the vine's roots, a clay saucer sits unglazed and unfired, shaped by Wren's own palms the week the lake drained. A thread of damp rises into it from the fissure Isolde's reed was pushed through, and the saucer has never been dry since.

**Constraint:** The saucer rests on the exact patch of ground where the vine's single gourd can only ripen if no one stands, so for Wren to carry the seed to it, she must descend the ladder, and the moment her weight is on the clay the vine stops bearing, which means the seed would be planted in the one year the town gets no gourd to show whether the planting worked.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The vine's roots have grown down through the saucer's unfired clay and out the bottom, and in the fissure below they have wrapped around Isolde's reed, so the plant drinks from the same thread of damp that feeds the jar, though no one in Vell Harrow has ever seen the roots.

**Constraint:** The roots draw so much of the seep that the saucer stays damp only because the vine is thirsty enough to pull the water up through it, so if Wren plants the seed there and it sprouts, the young plant will compete with the vine for that one thread, and the saucer will go dry and kill whichever of the two drinks less.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren's shawl has a second hem, stitched inside the first, holding a single hair from the ladder's original rope, the one woven before anyone had a reason to refuse to donate, and it is dyed with a pinch of the same ash that colors Hollis's cloths and Wren's knotted cord.

**Constraint:** The hair is the only thing in Vell Harrow that has touched every part of the town without being burned, rinsed, or sealed, but it is also the thread that would have to be pulled from the hem to bind the seed to the saucer, and pulling it unravels both hems at once, so the shawl falls apart and the seed drops out before it ever reaches the ground.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Beneath the shawl's outer hem, Wren has pinned a small bone needle that belonged to Quast. Its eye is threaded with a single strand of the same black oak fiber that the first stilt was cut from, and the needle has never once been used to sew.

**Constraint:** The needle was made to pass through only one material, the wet clay of the lake bed, and it snaps if driven through anything dry. Everything in Wren's shawl is bone dry, so the needle can never stitch the hair back into place until the seed has already reached the ground, and by then the shawl has no reason to be mended.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The black oak fiber in the needle's eye is the one thread in Vell Harrow cut from a living stilt rather than a dead one. Quast shaved it from the pillar's inner heartwood the night before he sealed his log, and the wood bled a clear sap where he cut, which has since hardened into a amber bead at the needle's tip.

**Constraint:** The bead is the only thing that keeps the fiber from fraying, but it melts at the exact warmth that lingers after a lightning strike on the collar, so the one night the needle might finally be wet enough to use, the storm's own heat will dissolve the bead and the thread will come apart in Wren's fingers before she reaches the clay.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Quast left a second needle, identical to the first, pushed point-first into the heartwood of the black oak stilt itself, just below the collar. It is threaded with a fiber of Marrow's grey hide, and its eye has been sealed shut with the same clear sap, now hardened into amber.

**Constraint:** The needle can be reached only from the clay directly beneath the collar, where a person must lie on their back, and Isolde is the one who lies there every storm night. But the needle sits exactly where the lightning enters the iron, so any hand that closes on it in the moment of the strike is the same hand that is feeling for which symbol was taken, and cannot do both.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Isolde has never reached for the needle. Instead she has pressed her left thumb against the bark beside it on every storm night for thirty years, and the wood there has worn into a smooth, shallow hollow the exact size of her thumb, warm to the touch for an hour after each strike.

**Constraint:** The hollow is deepest where her thumb rests most heavily, and she presses hardest during the strike itself, when the warmth is greatest and the fear is greatest. That means the shape of the dent records how frightened she was on each storm night, not which symbol was taken, and the two can no longer be separated, because the lightning that scorches a symbol is also what makes her press.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Directly above Isolde's thumb-hollow, the black oak bark carries a ring of tiny pale lichen, a species found nowhere else in Vell Harrow. It grows only where the stilt is warmed by lightning, and it has spread one thin ring outward for every storm in the thirty years she has lain beneath it.

**Constraint:** The lichen feeds on the same trace of warmth that the strike leaves behind, but it also dies from direct touch, and Isolde's thumb is the only thing that touches that bark. Each ring she presses against is therefore the one that withers soonest, so the lichen keeps the count of the storms, and her hand keeps erasing the most recent ones.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren's slow climbing has worn a pale stripe down the side of the lowest rung, and in the grain of that stripe a second species of lichen has taken hold, one that grows only where something moves too slowly to disturb it. **Constraint:** This lichen survives only while the rung stays in shade, but the black oak pillar's long shadow shortens a little each year as the Tanner residence settles and tilts. turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Wren's lowest rung is the only part of the ladder that was never woven from hair. **Constraint:** The hide stretches by a fraction under every climber, and it has never been allowed to rest, because the ladder is lowered each dawn and hauled up each dusk, so the rung is always loaded or being hauled. turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The sling was cut to fit the wrist of a nine-year-old, and Wren's wrist, thinned by age, now slides through it so easily that it holds her only when she is perfectly still. turns.text:

**Constraint:** The collar was fitted so tightly that it squeezes the glass, and the squeeze deepens a hair each year as the copper cools and contracts in the dry winters. turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A

turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B

turns.speaker: A

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Odalie Fenn's breath is dry because she keeps a pebble of desiccated lake salt under her tongue, a habit she took up as a girl to stop herself from speaking aloud to the Sull, and she has not been seen without the faint white crust it leaves at the corner of her lips.

**Constraint:** The salt dissolves a little with every word she says, so she can blow the bone flute dry only while holding her tongue perfectly still, and since the pitch must be compared against the spare spiral's note, which she can confirm only by speaking its name to Hollis, she must choose between hearing the flute's pitch and keeping the salt that makes the hearing possible.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The fork rings true only when it is struck on the parapet's brass sighting ring, and every strike knocks the ring off its alignment with the horizon, so each time Hollis confirms a pitch for Odalie he must spend the next four-minute window re-setting the ring instead of using the lens.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The fluff stays soft only while it sits in the cellar's still damp air, and Pip carries the pillow up to her bedroom each evening, where the dry air stiffens it a little more every night, so the pillow is slowly changing from a thing that swallows pitch into a thing that rattles it, and her hum will begin to carry a buzz that no one has ever heard from the Quiet Bell.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The beat comes only from the pillow's stiffening sedge, which is drying faster than the ledger's ink, so by the time Hollis has enough pulses to see a pattern, the fluff will have gone brittle and stopped buzzing, and the column will hold a rhythm that no longer comes from anything he can still hear.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The cord holds its twist only while the ledger stays shut, and Hollis must open it to log each new pulse, so every entry he writes loosens one strand of the very spine whose seven-fold count might have explained the numbers he is writing down.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The kinks lie flat whenever the thread is pulled taut enough to cut, and Hollis cannot slip a blade under it without drawing it tight, so the moment he could read the thread's count of sevens is the moment it stops showing any.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** A pale second thread runs parallel to the first inside the back cover, a strand of Hollis's grandfather's own white hair, sewn in loose so the binder could tell the two apart by touch, and it carries no kinks at all.

**Constraint:** The white hair is slack precisely because it was never meant to bear any load, so when Hollis draws the Marrow thread taut to cut it, the white one stays slack and curls away from the blade into the fold of the spine, where the only way to find it again is to open the ledger flat and strain the cord he is trying to spare.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

**Constraint:** The taper points toward the page's gutter, which is the one place Hollis can never read without breaking the binding, so the direction the stroke was drawn can be learned only by splitting the ledger flat, and the splitting would tear the very margin that holds the stroke.

turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:

turns.text:

**Constraint:** The widow set the wheel in a sealed window niche in the Marne rooftop shelter, directly beside the ledger, and its brass is coated in a lacquer that gives off a faint vapor as it ages. turns.text:

turns.text:

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** The rubbing was pressed with a thin skin of lampblack rubbed into the wax. The numerals therefore stand out in dark relief, and each night Pip's cheek presses them a hair's breadth deeper into the pillowcase's linen, where they leave a faint mirrored print on the inside of the weave.

**Constraint:** The mirrored print reads correctly only from the underside of the cloth, and that side is stitched to the sedge-fluff lining. Pip's pillowcase can be turned inside out only by unpicking its seam, and the seam was sewn with the left-handed hitch that the peddler, the apprentice, and the bone peg's maker all shared. Unpicking it would destroy the only handwriting that is common to every clue.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The seam's hitch was knotted around a single strand of Maren's own dark hair, wound in as a thread of sewing silk, so the hand that closed the pillowcase was not the apprentice's but Maren's, copying a hitch she had learned by untying and retying the toggles' knots as a girl.

**Constraint:** Maren learned the hitch from a tangle she was never allowed to cut, so she tied it backwards, with the extra half-turn on the wrong side, and a backwards hitch tightens when pulled in the direction that would loosen the true one, so any hand that tries to unpick it the way the apprentice would have tied it will draw the seam shut.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Maren left a single loose end of her dark hair hanging from the seam, no longer than a barleycorn, and it is tucked under the pillowcase's inner flap where Pip's cheek never reaches, so it has stayed supple while the rest of the thread has dried stiff.

**Constraint:** The end loosens the backwards hitch only if it is pulled toward the pillow's foot, but the flap that hides it is sewn down at that very end, so reaching the strand means first opening a second seam, and that seam was closed with a stitch Pip has since picked at in her sleep, tightening it into a knot nobody in Vell Harrow has ever seen.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** The knot Pip has tightened in her sleep is a small round bead of linen no bigger than a lentil, and it rolls freely along the flap's edge, because her sleeping fingers wind the thread around it in the same seven-pulse rhythm that buzzes in her hum.

**Constraint:** The bead slides only while the linen is warm from her head, so it can be coaxed free of the flap only at the hour Pip is asleep on the pillow, and any hand that reaches under her cheek to work it loose will wake her, whose waking hum is the one pitch in the town that has never drifted.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text:
**Fact:** Pip's waking hum is held true by a small habit she has never mentioned to anyone: before she sings the note, she presses her tongue to the roof of her mouth and counts seven heartbeats, and the pause lets her hear the Quiet Bell's thud still ringing faintly in the bones of her skull.

**Constraint:** The ringing lasts only as long as the bell's last strike is fresh, so the true pitch is available to her only in the first minutes after midnight, and by the time she wakes at dawn the thud has long since faded, leaving her to hum from a memory that began drifting the moment she fell asleep.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text:
**Fact:** Pip keeps a small cracked ocarina of fired clay under her bed, which she made herself from a pinch of the lake bed's grey clay and which she blows once each midnight, just after the bell, so that its note and the bell's thud overlap in the floorboards for the length of a single breath.

**Constraint:** The ocarina was fired in the Marne hearth, whose ash goes into Hollis's ledger, and the heat left a hairline crack that slowly widens with each blowing, so its pitch sags a little flatter every midnight, and the only note it will ever hold exactly true is the first one it made, which no one heard.
